appraisal_events.evidence: Elle disait « mon père » à Forcheville... on n'osait plus devant elle prononcer le nom de Swann. ... « Je ne la connais pas », dit-elle [of Lady Israël, though she in fact knew her]. C'est que Gilberte était devenue très snob. ... elle avait prononcé au lieu de Souann, Svann... s'avilissant pour se rehausser: « On a raconté beaucoup de choses très différentes sur ma naissance, moi, je dois tout ignorer. »
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator directly exposes Gilberte's calculated realignment away from Swann's memory toward Forcheville and aristocratic favor, capped by an explicit false denial and a self-serving distortion of her father's name; the narrator names her outright as having become 'très snob'.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Car personne n'est à la fois plus simple et plus haut que Mémé. Vous le verrez ne pas vouloir saluer une duchesse qu'il ne trouve pas assez duchesse et combler un valet de chiens. »
appraisal_events.explanation: Within her own anecdote about the pilgrimage, the duchess explicitly praises Charlus as uniquely combining simplicity and loftiness, illustrated by his generous, unpretentious rapport with peasants.

status_effects.explanation: Gilberte is clearly diminished as the narrator exposes her dishonesty and explicitly labels her snobbery.
Despite the moral cost, her erasure of Swann and adoption of Forcheville's name lets her pass more smoothly among aristocrats, who now charm easily to her.
Swann's name and paternity are quietly suppressed in Gilberte's new life and even distorted in pronunciation, marking his exclusion from her presented identity.
Charlus is elevated by the duchess's explicit admiring characterization of him as both humble and exalted, illustrated by his generosity toward ordinary people.

ambiguities: The duchess's praise of Charlus ('personne n'est à la fois plus simple et plus haut que Mémé') is embedded in her own reported anecdote; it is uncertain whether the narrator fully endorses this characterization or merely reports it, given Proust's habitual irony toward Guermantes self-mythologizing stories.
